source.title: Selective Preference Optimization via Token-Level Reward Function Estimation
source.authors: Kai-Lai Yang; Zhiwei Liu; Qian-Qian Xie; Ji-Min Huang; Er-Xue Min; Sophia Ananiadou

page_placements.theme: Small models select training data or tokens for larger models

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops SePO as a selective preference-optimization method inspired by weak-to-strong generalization. Its weak oracle selects tokens, rather than producing the labels used to train the student in the claim. The reported evaluations do not compare the student with its weak supervisor or calculate PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper reports outcomes for SePO with weak oracle models, but does not test the claimed weak-label fine-tuning intervention or its PGR. It does not report a weak-supervisor performance value for these experiments. The reported weak-oracle comparisons and weak-data results are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: SePO borrows the weak-to-strong framing: a small DPO oracle selects tokens, and the strong policy is trained on the dataset's own human/GPT-4 preference labels. No labels come from the weak model. No weak-supervisor score, strong ceiling or PGR is reported. Results compare SePO with the base model and other preference-optimization methods, which makes this the study's own method performance (T4).
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that SePO beats baselines using 30% of tokens. They also claim small oracles effectively supervise policies with up to 16.8x more parameters, and that SePO extracts useful signal from weak out-of-distribution data. This is their framing of weak-to-strong; it is not measured as PGR.
record.recipe_differences: SePO uses a DPO-trained oracle to estimate token-level rewards and select tokens, then optimizes a policy on selected preference-data tokens with a contrastive objective; it does not fine-tune the strong student on labels produced by the weak supervisor. The paper reports no PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with oracle size (Figure 5 and Table 3); the authors also state that low oracle training-data proportions can harm performance and that the needed proportion rises with policy-model size. These are SePO settings, not sensitivity results for the claimed method.

fits_no_version.finding: Small DPO oracles (down to Pythia-410M) selecting 30% of tokens let 2.8B and 6.9B policies exceed their base scores and full-token DPO/SimPO. Policy scores rise with oracle size, with diminishing returns up to 12B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak models used as token selectors, not label providers, can steer preference optimization of larger policies; selection quality scales with selector size.

fits_no_version.finding: On lower-quality HH-RLHF data, SePO slightly improves LLaMA2-Chat-13B over base: Arena-Hard 13.63 vs 12.0, AlpacaEval LC 8.81 vs 8.4. Full-token DPO, IPO, RRHF and SimPO fall below base.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selective token training mitigates over-optimization on weak out-of-distribution preference data.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says the project is open-sourced but the supplied text contains no URL.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: For the weak-to-strong experiments, the paper reports task benchmark outcomes rather than weak-supervisor scores or PGR, so the results cannot establish whether the student beats its oracle. The Table 1 oracle assignment is stated collectively for the table rather than paired row by row. Several oracle-size results are presented in Figure 5 without tabulated values; only the values explicitly stated in the text are recorded here. The paper reports averages of three random runs for Figure 4, but no uncertainty intervals for the outcomes recorded above.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the reported weak-oracle/table results used here. Other Table 1 methods and GPU-hour measurements were not recorded because they are not outcomes for the weak-oracle SePO intervention relevant to the claim.

untested.parts: There is no strong model fine-tuned on weak-model labels, and no weak-supervisor baseline or PGR.
There is no training change to naive weak-label fine-tuning, and no PGR.
Oracle size is varied, but PGR is not measured.
The HH-RLHF out-of-distribution data result is not a PGR-under-shift measure. Neither supervisor exploitation nor error similarity is measured.
No theory on when a student must beat its supervisor is given. The study's theorems are about DPO token rewards.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T4/uses_without_test classification is confirmed. All rows stay ['none']. No verdicts are given because no version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on labels produced by a weaker supervisor is tested; no weak-supervisor performance or PGR is reported.
The paper compares SePO with preference-optimization baselines, not training changes to the claimed weak-label fine-tuning method.
Oracle and policy model sizes vary, but the paper does not measure PGR; it tests language-model preference optimization only, not the claim's PGR across tasks or representations.
The paper evaluates selective optimization on weak/out-of-distribution data, but does not measure the claim's failure modes or PGR under distribution shift.
No theory is given for when a student must beat its supervisor under the claimed weak-label setup.
